conflict_topics: whether alcohol may be stored/served in the shared flat
storage location for alcoholic drinks (fridge vs cooler vs room vs void deck)
who sets rules in the shared home / authority over shared living space
practical guest management (invited manager and colleagues)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concrete reasons (religious rule, managerial guest expectations, practicality of party flow).
Positions are repeated but each time with added justification or practical consequence (e.g., fridge contamination vs manager being escorted downstairs).
Agent C plays a mediator role by proposing alternatives (void deck) and reminding others of religious constraints.
No role confusion; speakers reference shared facts (who invited whom, what was previously agreed).
evaluation.final_reason: No affirmative agreement was reached. Agent D consistently objected to alcohol being served in the home for religious reasons; Agent A and Agent B insisted the original housewarming plan (with alcohol served in the flat) should proceed or at least not be split. Compromises were proposed (cooler for fridge, void deck, cooler in A's room). Agent D accepted the void-deck option (Round 7) for storage/serving off-site, but Agents A and B rejected that as unacceptable for running the party. The last proposal (Agent A offering to keep drinks in a cooler in her room) was not accepted by Agent D and does not resolve D's prohibition on alcohol being served in the shared home. Because the opposing demands (no alcohol served in the home vs hosting alcohol at the housewarming in the home) persist with no mutual acceptance, the conflict remains unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent D: Initially objected to alcohol in fridge and to alcohol being served in the home (Round 4, 9, 12). Softened on the storage/serving-location issue by accepting the void-deck option in Round 7, but did not abandon the broader prohibition on hosting alcohol in the home.

Agent A: Initially assumed the original plan stands and resists splitting the party. In Round 12 suggested storing drinks in a cooler in her room (tactical shift) but did not accept the void-deck compromise and has not conceded the right to remove alcohol from the home.

Agent C: Initially 'okay with it' (Round 7) but then became mediator proposing compromises (void deck) and defended Agent D's religious constraint (Round 9), showing a shift from passive acceptance to active mediation.
Agent B: Consistently concerned about guests (manager) and aligns with Agent A when compromises would embarrass or inconvenience invited guests; B did not change position.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1: Agent A asks 'So, are we all set for Saturday?' Turn 2: Agent B: 'Yeah, I think so.' No incompatible claims or demands expressed.
Turn 3: Agent A: 'Is the alcohol in the fridge okay with everyone?' Turn 4: Agent B: 'Yeah, it's fine with me.' No opposition voiced.

Turn 5: Agent A asks Agent C and D. Turn 7: Agent C: 'I'm okay with it, but we should check with Agent D. Will it be an issue with the halal food in the fridge?' This raises a potential concern but no incompatible demand yet.

Turn 9: Agent D: '...I'm not comfortable with alcohol in the fridge next to my food. And I also can't have alcohol served in my home. It's a religious thing.' Turn 11: Agent A: 'We can get a cooler... But what do you mean we can't serve alcohol? We all agreed to have a housewarming party.' Clear, substantive disagreement over whether alcohol can be present/served in the shared flat.

Turn 12: Agent D reiterates: '...As a Muslim, I can't host a party where alcohol is being served in my home. It's my home, you know?' Turn 13: Agent A counters: 'It's our home, Agent D. All four of us.' Positions about authority over the flat and permissibility of alcohol are strongly opposed and framed as non-negotiable.

Turn 14: Agent B raises a practical problem: 'I invited my manager...' Turn 15: Agent C proposes a compromise: 'What if we have the drinks downstairs? We could set up a table at the void deck.' A practical alternative is offered, reducing immediate friction but not settling the core dispute about serving alcohol in the home.

Turn 16: Agent D: 'Oh, downstairs? At the void deck? Yeah, that works for me.' Agent D accepts the void-deck storage/serving compromise. Turn 18: Agent A objects: 'So people have to go all the way downstairs for a drink? ...The party will be in two different places.' The original dispute over alcohol in the flat has been partly addressed (storage/serving off-site), but A objects to the practical effect.

Turn 19: Agent B: '...It's a bit strange to send guests downstairs to the void deck for a drink. I can't really do that to my manager.' Turn 20: Agent C: 'I know it's awkward. But it's a compromise...' Practical objections to the proposed compromise re-intensify the disagreement about how to run the party.

Turn 22: Agent A: 'The other option is what we all agreed to in the first place. Have the party here.' Turn 23: Agent C: 'But we didn't know it was a problem for Agent D back then. It's a religious rule.' The contest between maintaining the original plan and accommodating religious restriction continues with no agreement.

Turn 25: Agent A challenges authority: 'So her rules apply to the whole flat now? We all live here, Agent C. We all pay rent.' Turn 26: Agent C frames it as shared living necessity: 'It's not about her rules taking over. It's about us trying to live together.' The dispute about which norms govern shared space intensifies and becomes more entrenched.

Turn 27: Agent A: 'But this doesn't work for everyone. It doesn't work for me, and it's not great for Agent B's guests either.' Turn 28: Agent B: 'She's right, that doesn't work for me.' A and B align against D's constraint; polarization increases without resolution.

Turn 29: Agent C: 'But it didn't work for everyone. We just didn't know it then.' Turn 31: Agent A proposes: 'If the problem is the fridge, fine. We can keep the drinks in a cooler box in my room.' A new proposal is made but does not address Agent D's stated prohibition on alcohol being served in their home, and Agent D does not accept this suggestion in the transcript. The core incompatibility remains.

substantive_insights: Main tension is normative (religious prohibition) vs practical/social expectations (serving alcohol at a party, guest impressing manager).
Storage fixes (cooler instead of fridge) address contamination concerns but do not resolve the separate issue of hosting alcohol in a home held to religious rules.
The shared-tenancy ambiguity (Agent D calling it 'my home' vs Agent A 'our home') is a core source of friction about who may enforce rules.
Proposed compromises shift burdens (sending guests downstairs, or splitting party) that some housemates find unacceptable because of social consequences (Agent B's manager).
